articles.title: Satellite images verify new strikes on two Russian airbases
articles.body:
- Satellite images confirmed Ukrainian FP-1 drones destroyed an ammunition depot and maintenance facility and damaged two radars at Russia's Millerovo airbase on August 30.
- Separate imagery from a September 4 strike showed a destroyed Ka-52 and Mi-28 helicopter and a damaged Mi-8 at Sochi's airport.
Satellite imagery has confirmed damage to two radar systems, a maintenance facility and an ammunition depot at Russia’s Millerovo airbase in Rostov Oblast, following a Ukrainian drone strike on the night of August 30, according to images published by the Dnipro OSINT.
Ukrainian outlet Militarnyi reported that Ukraine’s 1st Separate Center of the Unmanned Systems Forces carried out the attack using FP-1 long-range strike drones, also striking Yeysk airbase the same night. At Millerovo, the satellite images show the ammunition depot and the base’s technical and maintenance facility, known by its Ukrainian abbreviation TECh, were completely destroyed, while an RSP-27 precision approach radar and a Nebo-SV early warning radar were both damaged.
Millerovo has been struck repeatedly since Russia’s full-scale invasion began. The base sits about four kilometers northwest of Millerovo city and has hosted Russia’s 31st Guards Fighter Aviation Regiment, which flies Su-30SM fighters, along with earlier deployments of Su-25 attack aircraft. Ukrainian officials have described the base as a key staging point for Russian frontline aviation supporting operations in eastern and southern Ukraine, and it was previously hit in drone attacks in December 2023 and July 2025.
The FP-1 is built by the Ukrainian company Fire Point and has become one of Ukraine’s primary tools for long-range strikes inside Russia. The drone carries a warhead of 60 to 120 kilograms depending on configuration, with a documented range of 1,600 kilometers, and Fire Point has said an upgraded model unveiled this year can reach as far as 2,700 kilometers. Ukraine’s military has credited FP-1 strikes with more than half of its long-range drone missions against Russian targets, including ammunition depots, oil refineries, radar stations and air defense systems.
Separately, satellite and visual evidence reviewed following a strike on September 4 identified damage to Russian military aircraft parked at Sochi’s airport in Krasnodar Krai, according to the same reporting.
A Ka-52 attack helicopter and a Mi-28 attack helicopter were destroyed, and a Mi-8 transport helicopter was damaged, at the facility’s military helicopter parking area. Sochi’s airport has been targeted in prior Ukrainian strikes, including an October 2023 attack that Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence directorate said hit a parking area for Russian helicopters in the airport’s Adler district, and an August 2025 strike that set fire to a nearby oil depot.
Russian authorities have not issued a public statement on either the Millerovo or Sochi strikes described in this report.

articles.title: Ukraine logged impacts at 11 sites while the American peace delegation was still in Moscow
articles.body:
Russia attacked Ukraine from 18:00 on 5 September and through the night into 6 September with 108 strike drones and S8000 Banderol cruise missiles, Ukraine's Air Force reported. The assault ran while US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were finishing three hours of talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow. They left the Russian capital after midnight and were expected in Kyiv on 6 September, again carrying a US proposal to end the war. Ukraine's own offer of a four-day pause in the fighting went unmatched by Russia.
The attack was still running in the morning
By 09:30 air defenses had downed or suppressed 82 Shahed-type, Gerbera, and other drones, along with six Banderol missiles. The military logged impacts at 11 locations and falling debris at seven more, and warned that Russian drones were still in Ukraine's airspace.
Over the previous day, Russian strikes killed seven people and injured 57 across Kharkiv, Kherson, Zaporizhzhia, Dnipropetrovsk, and Donetsk oblasts, according to oblast administration figures published on the morning of 6 September. Kharkiv Oblast lost four people, three of them one family in Chuhuiv. Zaporizhzhia Oblast reported one death, 25 injured, and 886 strikes on 54 settlements.
Three hours in the Kremlin
Trending Now
Witkoff and Kushner met Putin on 5 September and left the Kremlin close to midnight. Putin opened by telling them he had "full trust" in the US side, Axios reported, and Washington's goal is to restart direct Russian-Ukrainian talks that stopped six months ago. Putin's aide Yuri Ushakov called the discussion "substantive, constructive, exceptionally candid," ABC News reported, and stated the envoys had promised to carry Putin's own assessments into their meetings in Kyiv. Ushakov also repeated that Russia will achieve its goals and that the war's "root causes" must be removed — the Kremlin's shorthand for barring Ukraine from NATO and cutting down its army.
A White House official told RFE/RL that the sides discussed "concrete plans" for next steps, to be announced in the coming weeks. Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev, who sat in on the talks, called the Moscow trip an important peacemaking visit, Al Jazeera reported. The Kyiv leg would be the envoys' first trip to Ukraine since taking over the US effort; it was set for August and postponed as Russian strikes intensified.

articles.title: US Fighters, Drones Strike 3 Iranian Oil Tankers After Iran Fires on Navy Ships
articles.body:
The U.S. military struck three Iranian oil tankers on Sept. 5, as the Trump administration and Iran battle for control over the Strait of Hormuz.
A mix of Air Force and Navy aircraft carried out the attacks, including both fighters and drones, U.S. officials told Air & Space Forces Magazine. The attack followed an unsuccessful Iranian ballistic missile attack on a U.S. aircraft carrier and a guided-missile destroyer. Neither U.S. ship was hit.
“Let the message to the IRGC be clear,” said Adm. Brad Cooper, the CENTCOM commander, referring to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. “If you shoot at our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost—take out three of yours.”
Cooper’s statement continued: “We will not hesitate to defend American forces, and if necessary, destroy Iran’s limited and exposed oil fleet.”
The three Iranian tankers included M/T Downy, which was hit near Kharg Island, and the M/T Stark 1, which was struck near Jask, a coastal city in Iran. The M/T Downy and M/T Stark 1 were “permanently disabled,” according to CENTCOM. The third Iranian tanker, M/T Kylo, was hit in the Gulf of Oman. Struck in multiple locations, that tanker was rendered inoperable and “completely destroyed,” according to CENTCOM. It later sank. The Iranian crew was warned that it should abandon ship before the strike, the command said. CENTCOM released videos of the attacks on the ships and the sinking of the M/T Kylo.
The M/T Downy and M/T Stark 1 were impacted by weapons fired at the stern, while the M/T Kylo suffered a more significant bombardment.
The U.S. attacks on the Iranian oil tankers are part of a new Trump administration policy to deter Iranian attacks on U.S. military forces and commercial vessels. Previously, the U.S. had focused its attacks on Iranian military targets, such as radars and surface-to-air missiles.
Iran’s foreign ministry called the attacks on oil tankers a “war crime” intended to further America’s “economic war” on the Iranian homeland. Cooper said the attacks on Iran’s oil carriers are justified because they generate revenue for the IRGC.
The IRGC said in its own statement that it would follow suit and that it targeted “three oil tankers traveling through an unauthorized route in the Strait of Hormuz, as well as three vessels affiliated with the United States in other areas.”
The U.S. is seeking to use economic sanctions and a blockade to pressure Iran to give up its attempt to control international shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and to agree to limits on its nuclear program.

articles.title: US Envoys Head To Kyiv After  Stop In Moscow, Late-Night Meeting With Putin
articles.body:
KYIV -- After a day of crucial meetings in Moscow, including with President Vladimir Putin, US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have arrived in Kyiv for discussions with Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy with aims of ending the conflict now in its fifth year.
Ahead of their arrival in the Ukrainian capital, Russian state news agency RIA Novosti reported that the Moscow talks between the envoys and Putin lasted about three hours, with the US representatives departing for Kyiv shortly afterward.
A White House official told RFE/RL that "the two sides discussed substantive plans for next steps, which will be announced in the coming weeks" and that the envoys "look forward to equally productive meetings" in Ukraine on September 6.
As Kyiv prepared for their arrival, Zelenskyy said on September 6 that he had met with Ukraine's negotiating team ahead of the talks with the US envoys.
"We are ready for the conversation. Ukraine has always been and will remain constructive," he said on X, adding that Ukraine's proposals were ready.
Ahead of Witkoff and Kushner's arrival on September 6, Zelenskyy said on X that he had met with Ukraine's negotiating team to prepare for the talks.
"We are ready for the conversation. Ukraine has always been and will remain constructive," he said on X, adding that Ukraine's proposals were ready.
Later, Zelenskyy said the talks with Witkoff and Kushner had begun, posting a video showing the US envoys meeting with him and other Ukrainian officials.
As the talks in Moscow started late on September 5, RIA Novosti quoted Putin as saying the three men would have to address a "difficult situation" during their Kremlin discussions.
Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov, who participated in the session, called the talks "substantive, very frank, and constructive." He added that the envoys stated the US position and promised to present Putin's views to Ukrainian leaders during their talks in Kyiv.
"They not only expressed their traditional interest in bringing the hostilities to a quick end, they put forward a number of ideas on possible routes to a settlement," he said.
Ushakov insisted Russia would achieve its goals and that the "root causes" of the conflict must be resolved, Kremlin code for putting an end to Ukraine's hopes of NATO membership and steps to effectively disarm the Ukrainian military, among other historical grievances -- items Kyiv has long rejected.
Even as the diplomatic push continued, Russian forces launched another large-scale drone attack on Ukraine overnight into September 6.
Ukraine's Air Force said Russia launched 108 drones, including Shahed attack drones and jet-powered variants. It said air defenses had shot down or suppressed 88 drones by 9:30 a.m., while strikes were recorded at 11 locations and falling debris at seven.
The attack followed a day of Russian strikes across Ukraine that killed seven people and left 57 others injured or otherwise affected in five regions, according to regional military administrations. Four of those killed were in the Kharkiv region, including an 11-year-old boy.
As the United States pressed ahead with its latest effort to end the war, President Donald Trump had said his envoys would be presenting a peace deal to the Russians and then would relay the offer to Ukraine the next day.
Trump said Washington had "an idea for peace" and that his envoys were "bringing with them a proposal to end the war," now in its fifth year since Putin launched the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
"I sent them over to see whether or not we can get something done, and there may be a good chance that we'll do it," Trump told reporters on September 4.
'Diplomatic Activities'
The US envoys' visit to Kyiv would mark their first visit to Ukraine since taking leading roles in the administration's efforts to end the war and comes amid a renewed diplomatic push aimed at reaching a peace agreement.
Trump made ending the largest war in Europe since 1945 a priority when he took office in January 2025, but an agreement has been elusive, and diplomacy had been largely stalled since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran in late February.
Reflecting the hard-line stance put forward by Ushakov, Putin has shown no sign of compromise in recent comments, among other things insisting that Russia must control all of eastern Ukraine's Donetsk region, including the parts its forces have failed to capture in years of heavy fighting.
Before the envoys departed the US, Zelenskyy said Ukrainian forces would "ensure the normal functioning of Russia airspace so that the negotiators can arrive there safely" and demanded that Moscow reciprocate.
Following his September 5 call with the envoys, Zelenskyy said that "from now through the end of Saturday, as well as on Sunday and Monday, Ukraine is ready to refrain from strikes on Moscow."
Putin subsequently ordered a halt to strikes on Kyiv from September 6-8, according to spokesman Dmitry Peskov, who made no mention of other parts of Ukraine amid reports that Russia had continued its attacks elsewhere.
Flying into Kyiv would be highly unusual. Ukrainian airspace has been closed to regular civilian flights since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022, and visiting foreign leaders and officials have generally reached the capital by train.

articles.title: The only viable path — America must return to the agreement
articles.body:
The only viable path — America must return to the agreement
The Iran newspaper, in an interview with Mashallah Shakeri, former ambassador of the Islamic Republic of Iran to Pakistan, explored why Pakistan is once again attempting to mediate between Iran and the United States.
Shakeri explained that with the renewed outbreak of conflict between Iran and the US and the intensification of regional tensions, Pakistan has resumed efforts to play a mediating role. According to him, three main factors drive Islamabad’s approach: A mission assigned to Pakistan by the United States, indicating Washington’s desire for indirect channels of communication. Pakistan’s strategic interests and sensitivities regarding Persian Gulf states, which compel Islamabad to maintain balanced relations. Public opinion in Pakistan, where societal attitudes toward Iran are generally positive, creating domestic support for mediation. Shakeri stressed that any diplomatic initiative between Iran and the US will only be taken seriously by Tehran if Washington returns to the bilateral agreement previously signed. He added that the United States must fully implement its commitments within the agreement’s clear and defined provisions. Only practical, sustained US adherence can make the agreement acceptable to the Islamic Republic of Iran as a legitimate basis for future action.
Arman-e-Emrooz: Reducing external tension; the first step toward economic reform
Arman-e-Emrooz analyzed sanctions and economic pressures, quoting banking expert Kamran Nadri. Nadri stated that since the late 2000s, when nuclear‑related sanctions began, Iran’s economic conditions have steadily worsened. He emphasized that sanctions were not merely a political bluff; they have had real and measurable effects. For sanctions to reach their full potential, however, broad international cooperation is required. He noted that much of the discussion about intensifying economic pressure has already materialized in practice. Nadri argued that the war must be resolved first. After that, conditions for lifting sanctions can be created. Only then can Iran pursue deep structural reforms. He insisted that all political factions and the entire country must prioritize resolving the fundamental challenge of war and moving toward peace. Remaining in a prolonged state of tension is impossible, as it inevitably produces economic and social damage.
Kayhan: Europe’s deepening energy crisis
Kayhan focused on Europe’s worsening energy situation, arguing that Europe has fallen victim to what it calls “Trump’s folly.” According to the paper, reports show that the energy crisis — triggered by US and Israeli military operations against Iran — has pushed Europe’s gas reserves to their lowest level in 15 years just as winter approaches. This has heightened fears of another sharp rise in energy prices. Energy traders had expected prices to fall as tensions eased in West Asia and gas exports normalized. However, the prolonged war and continued supply disruptions have overturned those expectations. Europe now enters the cold season with significantly lower‑than‑normal reserves, limited time to replenish storage, and greater dependence on imported shipments, making it more vulnerable to price volatility and any new supply disruption.
Siasat-e-Rooz: Europe must be punished
Siasat-e-Rooz analyzed the European Union’s formal participation in the US -led economic exclusion campaign against Iran. The paper wrote that the EU welcomes efforts to ensure Iran halts destabilizing activities and engages in peace negotiations in good faith — including through additional economic pressure such as the US -led exclusion operation. However, the article argues that although Europe claims to be an independent global actor, its behavior reveals servility toward the United States and Israel, acting outside its own interests. The paper asserts that while the US seeks to demonstrate international consensus against Iran, Europe’s lack of autonomy actually reveals Washington’s weakness in building genuine consensus. The article concludes that the time has come for Iran to increase pressure — including maintaining strict control over the Strait of Hormuz and preventing energy exports to Europe, so that Iran can punish Europe decisively.
Etemad: Stabilizing deterrence and blocking CENTCOM’s strategy
Etemad reported on US attacks against Iran and Iran’s forceful response. Following US airstrikes on areas in southern and southwestern Iran, Iran’s armed forces launched their largest and most coordinated retaliatory operation since the ceasefire. They targeted five US military bases and command centers in Jordan, Kuwait, Erbil (Iraq), and Bahrain using a combination of missile and drone attacks. According to the paper, Iran’s retaliatory operation delivered a clear strategic message to the White House: “The era of one‑sided attacks is over.” By precisely striking five strategic US installations, Tehran significantly increased the cost of any further American military action.

articles.title: EU member refuses to point finger at Russia over German drone incident
articles.body:
EU member refuses to point finger at Russia over German drone incident
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev has refused to assign blame for last month’s drone incident in Germany squarely to Russia, citing “reckless” Western weapons deliveries to Kiev.
Earlier this week, the German government said it had grounds to believe that Moscow was behind the incident, in which an explosive-laden UAV was found between Ukrainian Antonov cargo planes at Leipzig/Halle Airport on August 4.
Berlin subsequently announced the closure of the Russian Consulate General in Bonn and the Russian House in Berlin, as well as tighter border controls for Russian citizens. Moscow responded by shutting down the Goethe Institute centers in Moscow, St. Petersburg, and Ekaterinburg, which promote German language and culture.
Moscow has rejected the allegations, with President Vladimir Putin suggesting they were being used as a diversionary tactic to distract Germans from domestic economic woes.
While multiple fellow EU member states have issued statements backing Germany’s position, not all of them have jumped on the bandwagon of pointing the finger at Russia.
A case in point is Bulgaria, whose prime minister told the parliament on Friday that European shipments of long-range weapons to Ukraine have been just as “reckless” as the failed sabotage attempt in Germany last month. Radev pointed out that Kiev is using Western-made weaponry, backed by European intelligence and instructors, to conduct strikes deep inside Russian territory.
“And what can we expect when we attack deep inside another country with our long-range weapons? Will it stand by or will it respond?” the Bulgarian prime minister inquired rhetorically.
He went on to warn that the West’s insistence on achieving a “conventional military victory” over a major nuclear power is dramatically raising the risk of uncontrolled escalation with Moscow.
“Europe can exist without Russia, but Europe will hardly exist for long against Russia,” Radev concluded, calling on the EU to “sit down at the negotiating table [with Moscow] as soon as possible.”
Meanwhile, a number of prominent political figures in Germany have called into question the government’s response to the drone incident and, more broadly, Berlin’s current hostile policies toward Russia.
In a post on X on Wednesday, veteran left-wing politician Sahra Wagenknecht wrote that “even if Russia were behind it, a drone that caused no damage whatsoever is no reason to fuel a highly dangerous escalation that could end in a war with Russia, costing millions of lives.”
Similar assessments have been voiced by those at the opposite end of the political spectrum. Fielding questions from The Pioneer media outlet on Tuesday, Ulrich Siegmund – the lead candidate for the right-wing Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in Sunday’s regional elections in Saxony-Anhalt – said that a “continuous sequence of events” had led up to the drone incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport. He cited his country’s ever-deeper involvement in the Ukraine conflict, arguing that “it’s only logical that there will be some kind of reaction at some point.”
Siegmund criticized the anti-Russian policies pursued by successive German governments since the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022, saying that weapons deliveries to Kiev and economic sanctions against Moscow have done little to resolve the conflict and save people’s lives.
The AfD politician insisted that it was high time Germany engaged earnestly in diplomacy with Russia instead.

articles.title: US aircraft carriers within Iran's reach
articles.body:
Amid the intensifying military confrontation between Iran and the United States, the news of Iran firing ballistic missiles at a US aircraft carrier and a destroyer is not merely a development on the battlefield; it could be a sign of a shift in the operational environment for American forces and an increase in the cost of Washington's military presence in the region's waters.
The US Central Command (CENTCOM) has announced that the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) fired ballistic missiles at a US aircraft carrier and a guided-missile destroyer, and that these vessels managed to survive several attacks. According to the American account, none of the US forces were harmed in these attacks.
At first glance, the most important question might be whether the missiles actually struck the American ships. But from a strategic perspective, the significance of this development goes beyond the extent of direct damage. The more important issue is the change that such attacks can create in the calculations of American commanders regarding the level of security and freedom of action of US naval vessels in the region.
An aircraft carrier is one of the most important instruments of US military power projection beyond its borders. By deploying an aircraft carrier and its accompanying strike group, Washington in effect moves a portion of its air and naval power to the closest possible point to a crisis. This presence is intended to create deterrence, strike capability, and the ability to react quickly for the United States.
But this same feature also brings a vulnerability; the closer a carrier is to a conflict zone, the more important its protection becomes, and more resources must be allocated to defend it.
A carrier strike group is not limited to the carrier itself. A collection of destroyers, air defense systems, fighter jets, early warning and reconnaissance aircraft, and other military equipment are responsible for its protection. Therefore, a missile threat against an aircraft carrier effectively means challenging a vast defensive network.
From this angle, even if the launched missiles are intercepted and no damage is inflicted on the carrier, the attack itself can have operational consequences. Because American commanders must assume that their vessels are within range and that any presence in the region faces the possibility of attack. This is what can be called the "cost of presence."
To change the other side's calculations, Iran does not necessarily need to destroy a US carrier in every attack. Increasing the cost of protecting carriers, limiting their freedom of movement, changing the operational distance, increasing the need for reconnaissance, and creating psychological pressure on forces deployed in the region can also be part of the deterrence objective.
In modern warfare, a weapon is sometimes effective when it forces the opposing side to engage a large set of resources and equipment to counter it. From this perspective, a ballistic missile is not just a tool for inflicting damage; it can also be a tool for changing the operational behavior of the opposing side.
Of course, one should not conclude from this incident that the military balance between Iran and the United States has changed. The United States still possesses significant superiority in various military, intelligence, air, and naval domains, and its aircraft carriers have multiple layers of defense. Therefore, a distinction must be made between the "ability to target" and the "ability to destroy" a military target.
What matters now is the repeatability of this threat. If American forces conclude that the presence of aircraft carriers in certain areas continually exposes them to missile attacks, they will be forced to review their deployment and operational patterns.
In such circumstances, the distance of carriers from coastal areas, their movement patterns, the level of escort, the number of protective fighter jets, and the volume of reconnaissance operations could change. Each of these changes would mean an increase in operational costs for the United States.
On the other hand, the US response is also noteworthy. Washington will attempt to show, by responding to Iranian military and economic targets, that attacking US forces will not remain without cost. This approach could lead to the formation of a dangerous cycle of attack and response; a cycle in which each military action pushes the other side toward a more severe reaction.
Meanwhile, the region's waters are gradually becoming one of the main arenas of competition. The importance of this issue is not limited to military operations. The security of shipping, energy transit, oil tankers, and trade routes are also directly affected by this confrontation.
In such an environment, Iran enjoys an important geographical advantage. The proximity of the operational theater to Iran's coasts means that Washington cannot separate the issue of protecting its naval forces from the geographical conditions of the region.
In contrast, the United States will try to neutralize this advantage by relying on its air and naval superiority and defense systems. For this reason, the battle between the two sides is not only a battle of missiles against ships; it is also a battle over the calculation of the costs and benefits of continued military presence.
If Iran can increase the cost and risk of the US military presence without needing to inflict direct and widespread damage, it will have achieved part of its deterrence objective. On the other hand, if the United States can continue to keep its carriers deployed in the region and simultaneously use them in military operations, Iran's effort to limit Washington's freedom of action will face greater difficulty.
Ultimately, the importance of the recent news should not be summarized merely as "whether the missiles hit the American ship or not." The real significance is that a US aircraft carrier, which is a symbol of Washington's power and military presence in distant regions, must now operate in an environment where the missile threat against it has become a serious variable in operational calculations.
This development could be one of the most important signs of a changing deterrence equation in the region; an equation in which military power is not measured only by the amount of weaponry, but also by each side's ability to impose costs, increase risk, and limit the other side's freedom of action.
In such circumstances, the future of the US carrier presence in the region will become more than ever a strategic issue; because as the cost of protecting these carriers increases, the question of the benefits of their continued presence will also become more serious for American decision-makers.
MNA

articles.title: Germany Unveils Anti-Sabotage Plan After Leipzig Airport Attack
articles.body:
Germany is preparing a comprehensive package of domestic security measures to counter Russian sabotage, cyberattacks, and hybrid threats following an attempted explosive drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport, Bild reported.
German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt announced that Berlin is planning robust countermeasures covering drone defense, the protection of critical infrastructure, cyber resilience, and enhanced surveillance to detect spies and potential terrorists.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Russia’s hybrid attacks using explosive drones against airports, agents in our cities, cyberattacks on our networks, and sabotage of our infrastructure are a daily reality,” Dobrindt said. “These attacks will intensify, but we can fight back and defend ourselves.”
Under the proposal, Germany will expand the Federal Police’s mobile anti-drone capabilities. Rapid-reaction units equipped with specialized vehicles and helicopters will be stationed across nine key cities: Frankfurt am Main, Munich, Hamburg, Berlin, Stuttgart, Düsseldorf, Leipzig, Hanover, and Cologne.
Their operational remit will cover the protection of airspace over key transit hubs, airports, major railway stations, and the government quarter in Berlin, with the technical ability to intercept and neutralize explosive-laden drones.
The plan also grants critical infrastructure operators – including water utilities, energy companies, and defense manufacturing plants – expanded legal authority to actively counter and neutralize unauthorized drones without waiting for state law enforcement to arrive.
US Sanctions Chief Joins Moscow Talks as Putin Cites War Goals
Additionally, Berlin intends to deploy artificial intelligence tools, biometric facial recognition, and automated video surveillance at transport hubs to detect weapons, identify suspicious conduct, and track individuals suspected of espionage.
To guard against digital intrusion, Germany plans to establish a national “Cyberdome,” a distributed digital sensor network designed to detect and block coordinated cyberattacks.
Baltic shadow fleet pressure and rising sabotage wave
The domestic security initiative coincides with broader efforts by Berlin to apply economic and regulatory pressure against Moscow following the Aug. 4 drone incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport.
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul and Interior Minister Dobrindt publicly attributed responsibility for the airport attack directly to the Russian state, a stance endorsed across governing coalition parties. Siemtje Möller, foreign policy spokesperson for the Social Democratic Party (SPD) parliamentary group, affirmed that directly naming Russia was the correct course of action.
According to the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung (FAZ), German authorities are evaluating punitive measures targeting Russia’s maritime “shadow fleet” in the Baltic Sea. Officials are exploring stricter administrative, inspection, and legal mechanisms to impede or halt the transit of tankers used by Moscow to circumvent international sanctions.
The heightened security alerts follow a confidential assessment by Germany’s Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA), which recorded 165 suspected sabotage cases, 24 espionage investigations, and 747 suspicious drone flights nationwide during the first eight months of 2026.

articles.title: Iran threatens to expand strikes if US keeps 'harassing' its ships
articles.body:
Iran’s top joint military command warned Saturday that its strikes could expand if the United States continues what Tehran called the “harassment” of Iranian ships, in the latest sign that the confrontation between the two countries may be entering a more dangerous phase.
The warning, carried by Iranian state media, came amid a sharp escalation at sea after U.S. forces struck three Iranian crude oil tankers following ballistic missile fire by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps at two U.S. Navy warships.
U.S. Central Command said a U.S. aircraft carrier and a guided-missile destroyer successfully evaded multiple Iranian attacks and that no American personnel were harmed.
CENTCOM then said American forces permanently disabled the M/T Downy off Kharg Island and the M/T Stark 1 near Jask, while completely destroying the unladen M/T Kylo, also known as the Noxen, in the Gulf of Oman after ordering its crew to abandon ship.
“Let the message to the IRGC be clear: If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost, taking out three of yours,” CENTCOM commander Adm. Brad Cooper said.
“We will not hesitate to defend American forces, and if necessary, destroy Iran’s limited and exposed oil fleet,” he added.
The Iranian warning suggests Tehran is prepared to widen its military response if Washington continues targeting vessels tied to the Islamic Republic.
It also comes amid growing concern in Israel and the United States that Iran may deliberately escalate the confrontation in an effort to raise the economic and political cost of the conflict and pressure President Donald Trump back toward negotiations.
An Israeli official familiar with current assessments said Saturday there was substance to recent U.S. intelligence suggesting Tehran is considering a significant escalation. The official said Iran may believe time is working against it and could seek to create greater regional instability, including pressure on oil prices, as leverage over Washington.
The same assessment raised the possibility that Iran could eventually attack Israel directly or first use one of its regional proxies to wear down Israeli defenses and send a signal without immediately exposing Tehran as the direct force behind an attack.
Recent U.S. intelligence reporting has also suggested that Iran has grown more confident in its ability to strike targets across the Middle East after months of fighting and may be prepared to sustain the confrontation at least through the U.S. midterm elections.
That assessment has increased concern that further clashes at sea could become part of a broader Iranian strategy rather than isolated retaliation.
The latest confrontation around Iranian shipping follows renewed fighting near the Strait of Hormuz, where the United States has been escorting commercial vessels and striking Iranian military assets it says threaten freedom of navigation.
For Tehran, attacks on its oil fleet carry both military and economic significance. CENTCOM said the three tankers struck Saturday were part of a multibillion-dollar shadow network used to finance the IRGC and its regional proxies.
Iran’s threat to expand its strikes now raises the prospect of further attacks on U.S. naval forces or other American-linked targets if Washington continues targeting that network.
With both sides publicly signaling that they are prepared to impose higher costs on the other, the risk is growing that the naval confrontation could spill into a wider regional escalation.

articles.title: Ryazan Oil Refinery and Rostov Targeted in Drone Wave
articles.body:
Unidentified drones struck the Ryazan Oil Refinery and targeted Russia’s Rostov region early Sunday morning, Sept. 6, igniting a fire at the critical energy facility and damaging residential infrastructure.
The Ryazan Oil Refinery, one of the largest in Russia, caught fire following the drone impact, according to the Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The enterprise previously halted crude oil processing on July 29 after a Ukrainian drone strike confirmed by the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, as well as an earlier attack on May 15 that disrupted operations.
The facility processes roughly 13.1 million metric tons of crude oil annually – accounting for nearly 5% of Russia’s total refining capacity – and produced 2.2 million tons of gasoline, 3.4 million tons of diesel, and 4.3 million tons of fuel oil last year.
Concurrently, drones launched a sustained assault on the Rostov region, with local monitoring channels and media outlet Astra reporting that unmanned aircraft circled Rostov-on-Don for over four hours amid gunfire and helicopter response activity.
Footage from the scene showed a damaged multi-story residential building with displaced window frames across several floors, while explosions were also reported in the vicinity of a local Ozon warehouse.
Subsequently, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine confirmed that the Ryazan Oil Refinery, the Rostov-on-Don airfield, and three Russian air defense facilities had been struck.
“An oil refinery in Ryazan, Ryazan region, Russian Federation, has been struck. A fire has been reported on the refinery’s premises. The refinery is involved in supplying the Russian aggressor’s Armed Forces” .
Putin: The Cornered Rat
Additionally, in the Rostov region of Russia, the “Rostov-on-Don” airfield was struck. A fire was reported in the vicinity of the facility.
Earlier strikes on Sochi depot
The overnight operations follow a wave of drone strikes on Sept. 4 that targeted the Black Sea resort city of Sochi and the nearby Sirius settlement in Krasnodar Krai.
During those attacks, drones struck Rosneft’s Adler oil depot, sparking a significant blaze, while additional strikes in Sirius reportedly targeted positions housing Russian S-300 or S-400 air defense systems near Krylya Baltiki beach.
The targeted zone sits several dozen kilometers from Russian President Vladimir Putin’s Bocharov Ruchey residence, a property the Russian leader has reportedly avoided visiting amid recurring drone activity in the area.
Drone attacks earlier in the week also reached deep into Russian territory, targeting the Avangard defense plant in Sterlitamak, Republic of Bashkortostan, which manufactures explosives and ammunition components.
The broader campaign has created recurring disruptions around the Russian capital. On Sept. 4, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin claimed air defenses downed 35 drones approaching the city, prompting Russia’s Federal Air Transport Agency to temporarily halt flights at Vnukovo, Domodedovo, and Zhukovsky airports for a third consecutive night.

articles.title: Drones Attack Sanctioned Russian Vessel Lady Maria in Mediterranean Sea
articles.body:
Drones attacked the sanctioned vessel Lady Maria in the Mediterranean Sea, which is reportedly used to transport Russian weapons.
The NEVZOROV Telegram channel published footage of the attack.
The vessel was targeted by drones equipped with a system for dropping munitions. The strikes caused a small fire to break out on board.
According to data from the MarineTraffic vessel-tracking service, the ship departed the Algerian port of Oran and was headed for an undisclosed destination.
The latest route updates indicate that the vessel was sailing through the Mediterranean Sea, passing near the island of Crete on its way toward Syria.
The vessel Lady Maria (IMO 9220641) is currently under U.S. OFAC sanctions under the name STELLA-MARIA. The vessel has been linked to the Russian company MG-FLOT LLC (formerly TransMorFlot LLC) under the sanctions regime established by Executive Order 14024.
In addition to the United States, Ukraine also imposed sanctions on the vessel on May 23, 2026. The Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) stated that Lady Maria is involved in transporting military cargo and weapons for Russia.
According to intelligence reports, the vessel has been used on the Novorossiysk–Tartus route. It has also been linked to the transportation of weapons from Syria to Russia.
Other vessels operated by MG-FLOT LLC are also subject to sanctions. The company’s vessels have likewise been used to transport ammunition from North Korea.
There is currently no confirmed information on whether the drones were Ukrainian. However, the activity of Ukrainian intelligence and security services in these waters is not new.
In May 2026, Greek fishermen found a Ukrainian Magura naval drone near the southern part of Lefkada, an island in the Ionian Sea in western Greece.
In December 2025, the Security Service of Ukraine struck a tanker belonging to Russia’s shadow fleet in the neutral waters of the Mediterranean Sea for the first time.
Moreover, given that the vessel has been used to transport weapons to Syria, an Israeli strike cannot be ruled out. Israel has previously carried out attacks on Iranian ports, including Bandar-e Anzali on the Caspian Sea.

articles.title: Ukraine, NATO Chief Discuss Air Defense Ahead of Ramstein Meeting
articles.body:
Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara held a telephone conversation with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte to discuss preparations for the upcoming Ukraine Defense Contact Group meeting in the “Ramstein” format, the Ukrainian Defense Ministry announced on Saturday evening, Sept. 5.
During the call, Khmara and Rutte reviewed Ukraine’s priority battlefield needs, focusing primarily on securing additional air defense systems and expanding financial contributions for the Defense Forces.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Khmara characterized partner support across these two domains as Ukraine’s primary objective ahead of the multilateral summit scheduled for the coming days.
Khmara emphasized the necessity of consolidated allied assistance in strengthening air defenses, stating that Kyiv is counting on continued partner unity and swift decision-making.
He highlighted the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) program, which facilitates the targeted procurement and delivery of critical armaments to Ukrainian forces.
The discussions with NATO leadership follow a separate phone call between Khmara and German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius on Friday, in which both officials coordinated preparations for next week’s Ramstein gathering.
The previous Contact Group meeting occurred on June 18 at NATO headquarters in Brussels, co-chaired by the UK and Germany.
Urgent Patriot missile requests
The consultations ahead of the Ramstein summit follow a request by Kyiv urging the European Commission to allocate several billion euros from the EU’s €90 billion ($105 billion) support loan to purchase PAC-3 Patriot interceptor missiles.
ISW Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, September 5, 2026
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced Ukraine’s request on Sept. 2 in Brussels prior to a meeting with Rutte, confirming that member states are actively reviewing the proposal.
The requested funds are intended to finance high-end air defense capabilities, particularly PAC-3 missiles, which serve as Ukraine’s primary countermeasure against Russian ballistic missile strikes.
The EU’s €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan has already disbursed €8.5 billion (roughly $9.9 billion) since June to finance drone and missile manufacturing, alongside procurement plans for European-built fighter jets.
Concurrently, the EU and Ukraine are advancing the “Freyja” project, an initiative aimed at jointly developing a European anti-ballistic missile defense system.
Kyiv’s air defense push follows Khmara’s address to EU defense ministers on Sept. 1, where he outlined pressing operational gaps. In response, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas acknowledged that interceptors are in short supply, urging member states to review existing stockpiles and consider transferring or selling Patriot missiles approaching the end of their operational service lives.

articles.title: Russia’s Putin tells US envoys Witkoff, Kushner that situation in Ukraine is ‘difficult’
articles.body:
Kremlin says Ukraine talks with US envoys were useful; no sign of breakthrough
- Russian President Putin held over three hours of talks with US envoys, calling them "highly useful" but showing no signs of a breakthrough in ending the Ukraine war.
- Putin praised Trump's efforts and assured negotiators' safety, while Russia continued missile strikes on Kyiv despite a temporary pause during the talks.
- A wide gap remains between Russia and Ukraine on peace terms, with Russia insisting on territorial gains and Ukraine refusing to surrender land, prolonging the conflict.
AI generated
MOSCOW – Russian President Vladimir Putin held more than three hours of “highly useful” talks on Sept 5 with two US envoys seeking a deal to end the Ukraine war, a Kremlin aide said, but he gave no indication of any breakthrough.
The aide, Yuri Ushakov, said Americans Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner “outlined a number of ideas regarding possible avenues for a settlement”. Ushakov did not say what these ideas were.
He said Putin had told the pair that Russia was making “real progress” on the battlefield, was confident of achieving its goals and stressed the necessity of addressing “all the root causes of the conflict”.
All these are statements that Moscow has made repeatedly in the course of the war, which has dragged on for more than 4½ years. The war has seen both sides intensify long-range air strikes in recent weeks, while the front lines remain largely static.
There was no comment from Witkoff and Kushner, who were visiting Moscow for the first time since January on behalf of American President Donald Trump. They flew out of Moscow soon after the talks and are due to meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Kyiv on Sept 6.
“The talks went beyond a mere exchange of views on resolving the Ukrainian crisis. Economic issues and potential major, mutually beneficial Russian-American projects were discussed in some detail,” Ushakov said.
“Overall, one can say that the negotiations were timely and highly useful for both sides.”
Putin’s investment envoy Kirill Dmitriev posted afterwards on X that it had been an “important peacemaking visit”. He and Ushakov were both present at the meeting.
Putin praises Trump’s efforts
In televised remarks at the start of the talks, Putin praised Trump’s efforts to end the war. Trump suggested on Sept 4 the US had a fresh proposal aimed at ending the war, but did not elaborate.
“Understanding that he is entering a difficult situation, he nevertheless does not stop his efforts to help bring about a settlement and to make his contribution to resolving the Russian-Ukrainian conflict,” Putin said.
He promised to ensure the safety of the US negotiators. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said earlier that Putin had ordered the Russian military not to strike Kyiv for three days because of their trip.
Over the previous 10 days, Russia had pounded the Ukrainian capital day and night with missiles and drones, including an attack on Sept 4 on the headquarters of the SBU security service.
Ukraine has inflicted damaging hits throughout the summer on Russian refineries, oil terminals and warehouses of online retailer Wildberries, in a bid to raise the cost to Moscow of continuing the war. Zelensky said Kyiv was prepared to refrain from strikes on Moscow through Sept 7.
A vast gulf in positions
A vast gulf remains between Russia and Ukraine on how to end the war, the deadliest in Europe since World War II.
A source close to the Kremlin, speaking before reports emerged of the trip by Trump’s envoys, said Putin was still intent on capturing more territory.
“There is no chance of reaching an agreement regarding the front line until Putin finishes securing the remaining part of the Donetsk region,” the source told Reuters, adding that the Kremlin leader was confident – based on reports from his commanders – that this would happen by the end of the year.
Western military analysts see such a possibility as remote, given Moscow’s slow rate of progress. Ukraine has refused to surrender land it has successfully defended at huge cost, and rejects such terms as tantamount to surrender.
The Kremlin said on Sept 4 the position that Putin set out in a speech two years ago – that Ukraine should cede the entire territory of four regions claimed by Russia and abandon its plan to join NATO – was “unshakeable”.
Since the last US-mediated peace talks between Russia and Ukraine in February, each side has intensified long-range air attacks deep inside the other’s territory, while the war at sea has also escalated. REUTERS

articles.title: Iran war likely to drag on for another six months, ex-US defense secretary warns
articles.body:
Donald Trump’s war with Iran is likely to drag on for another six months, Leon Panetta, the former US defense secretary, has warned, as the US president struggles to find his way out of the controversial conflict.
Panetta declared in an interview that the war with Iran – launched by Trump over six months ago – risks becoming another “forever war in the Middle East”, with no clear end in sight.
“It’s no mystery that the United States and Iran are caught in a terrible stalemate, in which there really are very few options available to bring this war to an end,” said Panetta, who also served as CIA director under Barack Obama, suggesting the conflict is on course to become “another failed war” in the Middle East “like Iraq and Afghanistan”.
“I think the likelihood is this war is going to continue for another six months without being resolved,” he added.
Panetta spoke to the Guardian days after the US army secretary, Dan Driscoll, abruptly resigned, departing amid the conflict, following reports of tensions with the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, over a series of firings.
US service members “are going to war at a time when there’s tremendous turmoil at the Pentagon, in the command structure, which really creates a sense that there’s nobody in charge”, Panetta, who served as defense secretary from 2011 to 2013, added. “And I just think that, whether it’s Iran, or whether it’s our adversaries, they’re now looking at the United States, and see weakness in terms of our ability to be able to really implement our military capability of defending our country.”
He said: “My biggest concern right now is we live in a very dangerous world, with the primary threats coming from China, from Russia, from North Korea, and from terrorism, and yes, from Iran as well. But what I’m concerned about is that we’re sending a message of weakness to our primary adversaries.
“And while they continue to meet and support each other in this axis that’s been created, I think they look at the United States as being particularly weak right now, and that’s a horrible message to send at a time when we’re facing those kinds of threats.”
In a statement, the Pentagon insisted it was “firing on all cylinders” under Hegseth’s leadership.
“The premise that the Department is in disarray is completely baseless and an insult to every dedicated professional and warfighter in this building who comes to work every day to defend this nation,” the chief Pentagon spokesperson, Sean Parnell, said. “This is what reform looks like.”
The White House was also contacted for comment.
In March, just three weeks after the US and Israel launched their military operation in Iran, Panetta told the Guardian he believed Trump was stuck between a “rock and a hard place” as he weighed whether to expand the war in a bid to eliminate Iran’s leverage over the strait of Hormuz, or “just simply walk away and declare victory”, despite the risk of perceived failure.
Earlier this week Panetta said he “absolutely” believed Trump remains in that position. “He’s boxed himself in,” he said.
Trump now has three options, according to Panetta. The first would be to walk away and “admit that it’s a failed war”, something Panetta finds it difficult to see Trump doing.
The second would be to draw out the current “stalemate, with periodic attacks going back and forth, tit for tat”, and both sides attempting to “avoid the startup of a more dangerous war” while refusing to either negotiate or surrender.
That approach, Panetta believes, would produce “what all parties feared”: another protracted war in the Middle East.
The third option, he said, would be for the US to take control of the strait of Hormuz, and remove Iran’s “most dangerous leverage point” over the US, “which is the ability to to close and disrupt” the global trade chokepoint.
“So the president either steps up and does what’s necessary to open up the strait of Hormuz, or, as I said, he just continues to play this this game of pretending that somehow he’s winning a stalemate when the fact is he’s not,” Panetta said.
Asked if he believed the war is “winnable” for the US, Panetta replied: “It’s only winnable if there is a dramatic change in the attitude of the United States that makes clear that the objective, the primary objective by the United States at this point in time, is to reopen the strait of Hormuz.”
He also argued that Trump has damaged his credibility by repeatedly erroneously claiming that a deal to end the war is imminent, and that the strait of Hormuz is open.
“So the real question is, is he going to make a decision to actually deliver?” Panetta asked. “For a lot of reasons, right now, he’s caught in the worst of every world because not only does he not have credibility, but any threats he makes are totally ignored.”
Earlier this week, JD Vance told reporters that he would not describe the current military conflict with Iran a “war”. And asked whether he expected the conflict to be over by November’s US midterm elections, the vice-president replied: “I think the reality is I don’t know the answer to that question. You would have to ask the Iranians.”
Panetta told the Guardian he believes many Americans have “lost faith” in Trump’s “ability to handle this war”, pointing to recent polling that he said found that a majority of Americans believe that conflict with Iran was a mistake and are against it.
He also said he hopes the Pentagon and Trump’s broader administration learn from what happened with the extremely long deployment of the USS Abraham Lincoln, which arrived in Thailand this week after a record-breaking deployment supporting US operations against Iran that lasted more than 260 days without a port visit, amid reports of deteriorating living conditions and mental health aboard.
“Bottom line is, you do not deploy people endlessly into a war zone without making some kind of plans for rotation,” Panetta said.
“So it’s not just that the war is going badly – I think there’s also kind of a lack of trust in our military as to whether or not they are properly supporting our men and women who are putting their lives on the line.”

articles.title: U.S. attacks 3 Iranian oil tankers after missiles target Navy warships
articles.body:
U.S. forces struck three Iranian crude oil carriers Saturday after U.S. Central Command said the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps launched ballistic missiles toward two Navy warships in the region.
CENTCOM said it permanently disabled one crude oil carrier off the coast of Kharg Island and one near Jask. Another oil tanker was attacked in the Gulf of Oman.
The strikes come after CENTCOM said the Revolutionary Guard launched ballistic missiles toward two U.S. Navy warships patrolling the region. According to CENTCOM, a U.S. aircraft carrier and guided-missile destroyer successfully evaded multiple attacks, and no American personnel were harmed.
"Let the message to the IRGC be clear: If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost —taking out three of yours," Admiral Brad Cooper, CENTCOM commander, said in a statement Saturday. "We will not hesitate to defend American forces, and if necessary, destroy Iran's limited and exposed oil fleet."
Defense Sec. Pete Hegseth later wrote in a post on X: "It's simple: if Iran shoots at U.S. ships, we will destroy (and sink) their oil tankers, All they have to do is stop shooting at @USNavy."
There was no immediate response from Iranian authorities to Saturday's U.S. attacks.
Iran is the third-largest producer in the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and exported 90% of its crude via Kharg Island before the war. Flows have been disrupted by a U.S. blockade of Iranian oil exports, which began in mid-April.
The conflict between Iran and the U.S. has effectively shut the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for the world's oil supply before the war.
U.S. President Donald Trump threatened in June to seize Kharg Island as the U.S. continued military strikes against Iran. Most recently, on Aug. 31, he posted an artificial intelligence-generated video of Kharg Island being blown up.
The strike on the oil tankers comes a day after the Treasury Department announced sanctions against a small Turkish investment bank and two of its subsidiaries, which the U.S. accuses of facilitating funds for an arm of Iran's Revolutionary Guard.
The Treasury alleges that Golden Global Yatirim Bankasi Anonim Sirketi and its subsidiaries Golden Global Varlik Kiralama Anonim Sirketi and Golden Global Portfoy Yonetimi Anonim Sirketi were "established for the purpose of enabling Iran's rahbar network to transfer oil revenues from China to Turkey, where it could then be converted to cash and gold by rahbar money exchangers."
Golden Global Bank is the second major financial institution targeted under "Operation Economic Outcast," an effort by the Trump administration to isolate Tehran through non-military actions by sanctioning its business partners.

articles.title: US Destroys 3 Iranian Tankers After Warships Attacked in Gulf
articles.body:
The US military struck and disabled three crude oil tankers operated by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) after Iranian forces launched ballistic missiles at two US Navy warships patrolling regional waters.
According to a statement released by US Central Command (CENTCOM) on X, an American aircraft carrier and a guided-missile destroyer “evaded multiple unprovoked Iranian attacks,” with no US personnel injured and no damage reported to the naval vessels.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
In immediate retaliation, US forces conducted precision strikes against three IRGC-linked vessels. CENTCOM reported that American strikes permanently disabled the crude oil tanker M/T Downy off the coast of Kharg Island and the M/T Stark 1 near the port of Jask.
A third vessel, the unladen tanker M/T Kylo (also known as Noxen), was struck in multiple critical areas in the Gulf of Oman and subsequently sank, which CENTCOM later confirmed through released video footage.
“The three Iranian crude oil tankers are part of a multi-billion dollar illicit shadow network that finances the IRGC and its regional proxies,” CENTCOM stated. “Iran has no means to protect them.”
Thanks to the precision and professionalism of American service members, the M/T Kylo sank in the Gulf of Oman today and joined Iran’s navy at the bottom of the sea. pic.twitter.com/OwSDMl8SSQ
— U.S. Central Command (@CENTCOM) September 6, 2026
Following the strikes, the IRGC announced that it targeted six vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, claiming the group included three ships linked to the US and three commercial oil tankers.
According to Iran’s semi-official Tasnim news agency, the IRGC characterized the operation as retaliation for the US strikes on its tankers, alleging the commercial vessels had navigated through “unauthorized routes.”
US Envoys Hold 3-Hour Kremlin Talks With Putin
Iranian military authorities subsequently issued warnings to maritime traffic across the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, ordering vessels to avoid lanes not sanctioned by Tehran.
Escalation risks and threats to European bases
The direct exchange of fire marks a significant escalation in maritime hostilities amid stalled diplomatic negotiations to reopen the Strait of Hormuz shipping corridor.
The maritime clashes follow warnings from Iranian regime insiders that Tehran has considered expanding its retaliatory targets beyond the Middle East to include US military assets in southeastern Europe and Cyprus.
Insiders previously indicated that Iranian commanders evaluated potential strikes against facilities such as Bulgaria’s Bezmer air base – which approved refueling operations for US aircraft – and the British sovereign base at RAF Akrotiri on Cyprus, which was struck by an explosive drone in March.
Iranian planners have also examined targeting subsea fiber-optic cables traversing the Strait of Hormuz if hostilities continue to intensify.
The threats coincided with statements from US President Donald Trump warning that Washington would target Iranian domestic infrastructure, declaring the US would destroy a bridge or power plant in Iran every time Tehran attacks a ship navigating the strait.
While defense analysts note that Iranian medium-range ballistic missiles face accuracy limitations at extended ranges, Tehran’s rhetoric has grown uncompromising.
The appointment of hardline former IRGC commander Mohsen Rezaei as Iran’s top security official has underscored Tehran’s willingness to absorb higher risks and impose broader economic and military costs on Washington and its allies amid the breakdown of maritime transit talks.

articles.title: Live: Trump's envoys arrive in Kyiv after 'substantive' talks with Putin
articles.body:
American envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner discussed "substantive plans" for next steps to end the war in Ukraine during their meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow, the White House said, before they headed to Kyiv on Sunday. Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said the three-hour talks had been "highly useful" but gave no indication that a breakthrough had been reached. Follow our liveblog for all the latest updates.
European national security advisers are in Kyiv ahead of US envoy talks, Reuters reports
The British, French and German national security advisers are in Kyiv on Sunday, a person familiar with the matter said, ahead of talks between Ukraine and US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
The person did not specify which meetings the advisers would participate in.
Russia's Lavrov calls accusations of Moscow's involvement in Leipzig drone incident 'start of real war'
Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said on Sunday that the accusations levelled at Moscow by the West that it was involved in the drone incident at Germany's Leipzig airport were, "by and large, the start of a real war", state news agency TASS reported.
US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have arrived in Kyiv by train for their first visit to Ukraine for talks on how to end the war with Russia, a day after meeting Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow. It was Kushner and Witkoff's eighth visit to Moscow during the war, but it is their first in the Ukrainian capital.
Russia's TASS news agency reported early Sunday that Witkoff and Kushner flew to Rzeszow in Poland. Ukraine's airspace being closed since the war broke up in February 2022, TRump's men arrived in Kyic central station by train.
They are due to hold talks with President Volodymyr Zelensky.
Moscow and Kyiv exchange fire ahead of Ukraine meeting with US envoys
Russia and Ukraine continued to target each other with drone and missile strikes overnight into Sunday.
Moscow launched 108 drones and S8000 Banderol missiles at Ukraine, Kyiv's air force said, adding that it had shot down the majority of the drones and missiles and that 11 areas across the country had been hit by the bombardment.
For its part, Russia's military said that it had neutralised 258 Ukrainian drones fired at Russia overnight. Independent Russian media outlet ASTRA said that a refinery in the town of Riazan had been hit, sparking a fire.
In Zaporizhzhia, Russian drone strikes killed a 74-year-old man and wounded three people, while a drone damaged an apartment building, injuring seven people, in the Khmelnytskyi region, Ukraine's state emergency service said.
In Russia, a man was killed and a woman seriously wounded when a Ukrainian drone struck a vehicle, local authorities in the Belgorod border region said.
This handout photograph taken and released by the Ukrainian State Emergency Service on September 6, 2026 shows rescuers working at the site of a Russian strike in Kyiv region. Ukrainian State Emergency Service via AFP.
Zelensky calls for security guarantees ahead of meeting with US envoys
Russian President Vladimir Putin's investment envoy Kirill Dmitriev posted a photo of US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner leaving Moscow via Vnukovo International Airport on Saturday, hailing the meeting with Putin earlier that day as an "important peacemaking visit".
Dmitriev was part of the Russian delegation attending the meeting.
Moscow says it has not ruled out trilateral meeting between presidents of Russia, US, China, TASS reports
Russia's Deputy foreign minister Sergei Ryabkov said that the possibility of a trilateral meeting between the presidents of Russia, the US and China has not been ruled out, state news agency TASS reported.
But he said that before moving on to the actual preparations for the meeting, it was necessary to understand what its agenda will be.
"Here, the main question boils down to how the substance of the meeting will be formulated, and what we can expect as a result."
Earlier this month, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov raised the possibility of such a meeting between Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzen, China, in November.
'A bad sign': US envoys head to Kyiv after meeting Putin in Moscow
As US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner head to Kyiv following what the White House described as "substantive" talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin, FRANCE 24 correspondent Gulliver Cragg talks about what he describes as a climate of scepticism in Ukraine that these latest negotiations could bring a long-awaited breakthrough.
Witkoff and Kushner head to Kyiv after three-hour talks with Putin
Russian President Vladimir Putin met with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner at the Kremlin on Saturday for renewed talks on ending Russia's war in Ukraine.
The meeting, which lasted more than three hours behind closed doors, ended without announcements of any breakthroughs. Speaking to journalists afterward, Putin’s foreign policy adviser Yuri Ushakov described them as constructive, frank and useful, but didn't talk about specific outcomes.
Witkoff and Kushner are expected in Kyiv on Sunday.
Both Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky have agreed to pause strikes on each other’s capitals while the talks took place.
US envoys discussed 'substantive plans' for Ukraine with Putin, White House says
US President Donald Trump's business partner Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner discussed "substantive plans" for next steps toward ending the Ukraine war during their meeting Saturday with Russian President Vladimir Putin, the White House said.
The US envoys "discussed substantive plans for next steps, which will be announced in the coming weeks, and look forward to equally productive meetings tomorrow in Ukraine", a White House official said in a statement to AFP.

articles.title: US envoys head to Kyiv after talks with Putin
articles.body:
US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are due in Kyiv on Sunday for talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy after spending more than three hours with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow, as Washington seeks a route towards ending the war in Ukraine. The Kremlin and White House described Saturday’s meeting in positive terms but disclosed few details.
The White House said the meeting covered “substantive plans for next steps” and said further details would emerge in the coming weeks.
Witkoff and Kushner will now present the results of their Moscow discussions during their first wartime visit to the Ukrainian capital.
Putin’s foreign policy adviser Yuri Ushakov said the US representatives presented several ideas on possible routes towards a settlement. He did not disclose their contents. Ushakov described the discussions as useful and frank and said the meeting also covered economic relations between Russia and the United States.
“The talks went beyond a mere exchange of views on resolving the Ukrainian crisis,” Ushakov said. He said the delegations discussed economic questions and possible joint Russian-US projects.
The lack of detail left no public evidence of a change in the positions that have divided Moscow and Kyiv through previous rounds of diplomacy.
Putin told the US delegation that Russia remained confident about achieving its military objectives. According to Ushakov, the Russian president also repeated Moscow’s demand that negotiations address what the Kremlin calls the “root causes” of the war.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Russian forces occupy about one-fifth of Ukrainian territory. The ground front stretches for about 1,250 kilometres, with limited territorial changes despite months of fighting.
Moscow has continued to demand Ukrainian territorial concessions. The Kremlin said on Friday that Putin stood by terms he set out two years ago, including Ukrainian withdrawal from four regions claimed by Russia and an end to Kyiv’s plans to join NATO.
Ukraine rejects those demands and has refused to surrender territory that remains under its control.
A person close to the Kremlin told Reuters before the latest diplomatic mission that Putin intended to continue military operations until Russian forces had taken the remaining Ukrainian-held areas of the Donetsk region. The source said Putin believed Russian forces would achieve that objective by the end of 2026. Western military analysts cited by Reuters dispute that timetable because of the rate of Russian advances.
US President Donald Trump sent Witkoff and Kushner to Moscow after saying on Friday that Washington had prepared a proposal intended to end the war. Trump did not disclose its terms.
Putin thanked Trump for his diplomatic efforts when he welcomed the two representatives at the Kremlin.
“The situation is, of course, not simple,” Putin said in remarks shown on Russian television. He asked the envoys to pass his greetings and thanks to Trump before the closed meeting began.
Zelenskyy said on Saturday that he had already spoken with Witkoff and Kushner and was prepared for further discussions.
The diplomatic activity comes alongside continued missile and drone attacks.
Russian strikes on Saturday killed at least seven people, according to Ukrainian officials. Five people died in an attack on a factory in the Dnipro region, while strikes in the Kyiv area also caused deaths. Other attacks damaged buildings in southern and central Ukraine.
Zelenskyy said Russia had also struck airports in Kyiv and Boryspil before the US delegation’s expected arrival. He described those attacks as a Russian response to the possibility that the envoys would travel to Kyiv.
Ukraine’s airspace has remained closed to normal civilian traffic since the full-scale invasion began, and foreign delegations have generally entered the country by train.
Russia has agreed to suspend attacks on Kyiv for three days during the US visit. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Putin ordered the pause to protect the delegation.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine would refrain from strikes on Moscow through Monday.
“Ukraine is ready to refrain from strikes on Moscow, and we expect the Russians to do the same regarding Kyiv,” Zelenskyy wrote on X.
The temporary arrangement applies to the two capitals. No broader ceasefire has been announced.
Long-range attacks have increased in recent months. Russia has sent missiles and drones against Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities, while Ukraine has targeted Russian military sites, oil refineries, terminals and other infrastructure.
A Russian strike on Friday hit the headquarters of Ukraine’s SBU security service. Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries have disrupted fuel supplies and contributed to higher domestic fuel prices.

articles.title: Israel strikes southern Lebanon after Hezbollah launches drones at IDF troops
articles.body:
The Israeli Air Force launched a wave of strikes across southern Lebanon on Sunday morning after Hezbollah fired two explosive drones at IDF troops operating in the area. Soldiers intercepted one of the drones, and no Israeli casualties were reported.
Security officials said the launches were intended to stop or delay the IDF’s destruction of Hezbollah infrastructure on the strategic Ali Taher ridge, where Israeli forces recently completed a major operation.
Following an evacuation warning, the IDF struck a building in Arab Salim in the Nabatieh district. Lebanese reports said one person was killed and three others were wounded. A three-story building was also struck in Kfar Roummane, while Lebanese media later reported a strike on a motorcycle in Nabatieh.
Another strike in Nabatieh al-Fawqa hit a building belonging to Randor Hospital. Lebanese reports described it as a hospital building, while Israeli security officials told ynet it was completely empty and was being used as a Hezbollah command headquarters.
“The IDF is currently operating, and will continue to operate forcefully, against Hezbollah terrorist organization’s repeated attempts to harm our troops,” the military said.
Separately, the IDF announced a surprise General Staff exercise to test readiness for a sudden multi-front escalation. The drill is examining alert levels, the mobilization of forces and reserves, decision-making procedures and operational responses across the military.
The exercise was kept within a tightly restricted circle to surprise even senior generals and includes the rapid deployment of a battalion by helicopter. The IDF said increased movement of troops and aircraft would be noticeable across Israel, stressing that there was no actual security incident.
The military said the drill also incorporates lessons from fighting on multiple fronts and from the October 7 attack.
Hezbollah pressure over Ali Taher
Last week, the IDF said special forces had completed clearing the Ali Taher ridge of Hezbollah operatives. Security officials said no Iranian advisers or Quds Force members were identified there during the weeks-long operation.
According to the military, troops trapped Hezbollah operatives inside the compound, monitored escape routes and blocked outside assistance. Underground facilities included command rooms, weapons stores, generator rooms, living quarters, showers and a kitchen.
The IDF described the site as strategic infrastructure built over two decades with Iranian funding and planning.

articles.title: Putin says Russia has not struck Kyiv since midnight, but no broader ceasefire was agreed
articles.body:
Putin says Russia has not struck Kyiv since midnight, but no broader ceasefire was agreed
Russian leader Vladimir Putin has said during a meeting with US President Donald Trump's envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, that no strikes have been carried out on Kyiv since midnight on 5 September, but that Russia has never agreed on a broader ceasefire with Ukraine.
Source: Putin at the meeting with Witkoff and Kushner, as reported by Russian state news agencies RIA Novosti and TASS
Details: Witkoff thanked Putin for agreeing to the three-day ceasefire, during which neither Kyiv nor Moscow will be struck.
Quote from Putin: "We received this request through official channels – both intelligence channels and Foreign Ministry channels – to stop strikes on Kyiv. I issued the relevant order, and no strikes have been carried out on Kyiv since midnight.
I would like to note that the Ukrainian side has also significantly reduced strikes on Russian territory, including Moscow.
The Ukrainian authorities publicised their call for a broader three-day ceasefire, but we never agreed on that with them. But we will do everything in our power to ensure the security of the negotiation process and of the mediators represented by you and possibly by the people accompanying you."
Details: Putin also said he planned to discuss "all the modalities" of a settlement in Ukraine with Witkoff and Kushner.
Putin noted that Moscow is comfortable working with Witkoff and Kushner, and that this kind of contact is always beneficial.
Witkoff said talking with the Russian leader was one of the greatest and most memorable moments of his life.
For reference: Five air-raid warnings have been issued in Kyiv since the start of 5 September.
Russian attacks on Kyiv Oblast on 5 September have killed two people and damaged 28 properties in five districts.
Background:
- US President Donald Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived in Moscow on 5 September. They arrived at the Kremlin after a business lunch with Kirill Dmitriev, Putin's special envoy. The US negotiators are expected in Kyiv on 6 September.
- On the afternoon of 5 September, the Kremlin announced that Putin has ordered that no strikes be carried out on Kyiv for three days, starting from midnight.
- After speaking with Trump's special envoys, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated that Kyiv is willing to halt airstrikes on the cities involved in the negotiating process.
- Ukrainska Pravda reported that the Ukrainian authorities had sought to establish a temporary ceasefire along the line of contact ahead of the visit by Trump's special envoys. Ukraine's defence forces were ordered to observe a ceasefire from 00:00 on 5 September until 23:59 on 8 September. Russian forces thwarted this plan.
- Ukraine's General Staff later said that fighting is continuing along the line of contact because the Russians have not stopped their attacks on Ukraine.
- Kyrylo Budanov, Head of the President's Office, later confirmed that the ceasefire proposal had been conveyed to Putin, who had not responded.
